query: Which country controlled the dominions of Spain in North America
text: The dominions of Spain, in North America, were under the government of the viceroy of Mexico, and all her possessions in South America were subject to the control of the viceroy of Peru. In 1731, New Granada was divided, and a number of the provinces composing that kingdom were separated from it. These were put under the jurisdiction of a captain general and president, whose seat of government was at Caracas. text: A correspondent of the Standard writes from Salmon City under date of the 10th instant, as follows: At present the entire Yankee Fork country is dull and little is doing, owing to the deep snow and the consequent inactivity in the mines. Salmon City, in my opinion, is going to be a good town. The mines are rich and everything indicates a big rush here as soon as Spring opens. The roads are in a horrible condition at present, and nothing can possibly be done in the way of bringing in machinery for quartz mills before June or July, and until this is done the camp amounts to nothing. The snow lies in the streets, four feet deep on a level, and between here and Challis the road is filled in to a depth of 10 or 12 feet in a number of places. Everyone has great confidence in the camp, in proof of which there is not a lot within two miles of Salmon City that has not been taken up and fenced in, and you cannot buy them for love nor money, everyone bidding on for the Spring rush.

text: The WRoNG; LADY.-A Boston gentleman, whose lady was suffering from a cold, got up at midnight and went below to get a mustard poultice. In his hesitation he mistook the room on his return, and went into one where there was a light burning as dimly as that he left-a room altogether similar and apparently his wife in bed fast asleep. He applied the mustard poultice to her chest, and sat quietly awaiting at the bedside till it began to draw. It did draw; but it drew an infuriated scream from the young lady who had been the subject of his unconscious solicitude. At the sound of the unaccustomed voice, the nature of the accident which had befallen him and his patient was at once visible, and he rushed headlong from the arms of the mustard woman into the arms of his own. query: What occupation destroyed the original Celtic language
text: The degenerate inhabitants of South Britain, after the Roman legions withdrew, unable to defend themselves against the Scots and Picts of North Britain, applied to the German tribes called Saxons and Angles to come to their assistance and repel the Scots and Picts. The Anglo-Saxons accepted the invitation, drove out the Scots, but, in turn, reduced the natives to submission and took possession of South Britain, and held it until the battle of Hastings, in 1066, when the island fell into the hands of the Norman-French. During the 600 years of occupation by the Saxons, their language was substituted for the original Celtic. The Anglo-Saxons dropped the Runic and adopted the Roman alphabet, with a few alterations, and introduced it into Great Britain. It was during this period that the Saxon-German tongue became the vernacular of South Britain, literature, however, was in a crude state. Farmers can raise a few hills of broom corn each year, and having purchased one broom for $1.00, can make their own without the expense of buying. query: How deep did Professor Thompson and Dr Carpenter bring up deposits from
text: The general belief that the bed of the deep ocean is as far beneath the reach of direct examination by scientific men as the substance of the solid earth at the same depths has been dissipated by the success of some bold English investigators in directly exploring the depths of the sea. It appears that Professor Thompson and Dr. Carpenter, with the aid of a new contrivance for dredging, have succeeded in bringing up at different times loads of nearly half a ton of deposits from a depth of fourteen thousand feet (or two miles and two-thirds) below the surface. There are but three or four peaks in Europe which are higher above the sea level than the sea level is above the depths thus examined. The results of this examination have not yet been finally embodied in the sciences on which they bear, but enough has been published of them to show that some of the common doctrines of geologists and physiologists at least need revision.

query: In what country is mourning worn first in deep black
text: In France mourning is worn at first in deep black, and then gradually in gray, violet, and white. It is not worn as long as in England, and is more subject than in other countries to the rules of fashion and good taste. For deep mourning nothing has been found so satisfactory as Henrietta cloth, and this desirable material is shown at prices varying, according to quality, from $1 to $3 per yard. Notwithstanding the superior advantages of Henrietta cloth, many persons remain partial to bombazine, and this standard fabric remains at about the same prices as formerly— from $1.25 to $3 per yard. Next comes twillise cloth, and for summer wear it may be considered as especially desirable for the reason that it is very light and not requiring a lining, as is the case in regard to grenadine; it is really the cooler material of the two. query: How many boys have developed into eight before the carman has returned the second load
text: Before the carman has returned the second load, the one boy has developed into eight, each boy with a chair, each boy under feet, and each boy making as much noise as a planing mill on a calm day. The first wants two, he wants one under each arm. Then he starts down stairs. First the seats cross each other and nearly lay down, then they cross at the back, and the front ends fly off at a tangent, one of them tugging into the calcimined wall, and the other entangling in the banisters. But he won't let one of them go, but hangs onto both with exasperating obstinacy. In the meantime the carman, who is working by the load and not by the day, is waiting at the foot of the stairs, and wishing that he had that boy back of the Rocky Mountain for about fifteen minutes, with a straw bed for a y, and fan of dust at f. waiting to come down, and vociferating at the top of his voice, until the dust from the tick gets into his throat and precipitates him into a violent fit of coughing.

text: All the laws of trade are rejected as inoperative; the influence of supply and demand are treated as unimportant, while it is supposed that a parchment bulletin will suffice to keep the value of money uniform. The legal rate of money in New York is 7 per cent., yet in the last seven years, the market rate has varied from 24 per cent. to 5! per cent., and is now at from 6 to 7 per cent. In England the usury laws were abolished some years since, and in 1866 the Bank of England raised the rate of money, for the first time, to 6 per cent. It had never before, since the reign of Queen Anne, been over 5 per cent. That rate was maintained for a few months only, and for the last two years it has been at 1 1/2 to 2 per cent. In Louisiana the legal rate is 10 per cent., yet the market rate seldom reaches that point. The operation of usury laws is to raise the market rate of money beyond what it otherwise would be, were it like all other articles controlled only by the laws of trade.

text: I did an article headed "Coal," in which you state that the revenue derived from the mining of coal in the Cherokee Nation, during the past year, was only $7,000. This statement sur- prises me very much, as I am con- fident that there has been coal enough mined in Coowee-ooiwvee district alone and sold to citizens of Kansas, to have brought a thousand dollars into the treasury of the Nation if it had been properly attended to. It is evident that the officers of the district are at fault. They have either failed to collect the revenue or else have collected it, but failed to pay it into the treasury. I consider the coal question a very important one, and one our Council has sadly neglected.
